dedupe_keys.name: rand breaking glass missing hands workforce constraints on reconstituting lost us military space capabilities in 12 to 24 months 2026

description: This RAND Project AIR FORCE study asks how quickly the United States could rebuild satellites and supporting systems lost early in a protracted near-peer conflict, setting the benchmark for reconstitution at 12 to 24 months against the decade it usually takes to replace an ageing satellite. Alexandra Gerber, Jessie Riposo, Melanie Zaber and Bonnie Triezenberg published it on 31 August 2026 for the US Space Force. Coverage is the US space defence industrial base. Analysis of Bureau of Labor Statistics data and interviews find three shortfalls: engineers (about 3 percent of US engineers work in the counted space industries), technicians and assemblers, whose annual demand exceeds credentialed supply by nearly three to one, and advanced-degree specialists in electro-optical and radiation-hardening fields. It recommends scholarships, internships, vocational pipelines and fellowships, and automation as a resilience lever. Format and access: a free report page with a PDF; only the summary page was read. Licence: RAND permissions, not read. Caveats: US military focus, and the workforce counts rest on industry definitions that exclude aerospace manufacturing. It informs recovery and capacity planning for space infrastructure. A related catalogue record is the BEA US space economy statistics.

name: RAND Breaking Glass, Missing Hands: workforce constraints on reconstituting lost US military space capabilities in 12 to 24 months (2026)
outcomes: The space defence industrial base employs about 3 percent of US engineers, technician demand exceeds credentialed supply by nearly three to one, and clearance delays and foreign-national shares of doctorates constrain cleared talent, so a 12 to 24 month reconstitution benchmark is out of reach without Space Force investment in pipelines, training and automation.
